items.stem: A particular element (A) has one electron in its third shell. There is another element (B) with six electrons in its second shell. (i) How many electrons does A tend to give or take to become stable? (ii) What kind of ion would it form? (iii) How many electrons does B tend to give or take to become stable? (iv) What kind of ion would it form? (v) If A and B were to combine, what kind of bond would be formed? (vi) What would be the formula for the compound thus formed?
items.answer: (i) Element A has one electron in its outermost shell (electronic configuration 2, 8, 1). To achieve a stable octet, it will tend to give (lose) 1 electron. (ii) By losing one negatively charged electron, element A will form a positively charged ion known as a cation with a charge of +1 (A+). (iii) Element B has six electrons in its outermost shell (electronic configuration 2, 6). To complete its octet and become stable, it will tend to take (gain) 2 electrons. (iv) By gaining two negatively charged electrons, element B will form a negatively charged ion known as an anion with a charge of -2 (B²-). (v) Since element A transfers an electron and element B gains electrons to achieve stability, they will form an ionic bond (bond by electron transfer). (vi) The valency of A is 1 and the valency of B is 2. By crossing over their valencies, the formula of the compound formed will be A2B. 7.1 Mole in Terms of Mass 1 mole of a substance is the quantity of that substance equal to its ‘molecular mass’ ha grams. Here, the molecular mass has a general meaning, i.e., if the entity is atom, it is the atomic mass, if the entity is molecule, it is the molecular mass and so on. 7.2 Molar Mass It is the mass in grams of one mole of a substance. The unit of molar mass is g mol 1 - . 7.3 Molar Volume It is one mole of any gaseous substance at 1 atmospheric pressure and 273 K temperature which occupies a volume of 22.4 litres or 22400 mL. 8. Percentage composition of a compound The composition of a compound is expressed as mass percentage of each element present in that compound. Find the percentage of each element from the given data. We get percentage of oxygen by subtracting the sum of all other percentages from 100. Percentage of O = {100 – sum of percentages of all other elements} 2. Calculate the relative number of atoms by dividing the percentage of each element present in the compound by its atomic mass. 3. To determine the simplest ratio of atoms, find out the lowest value of relative number of atoms and divide each value of relative number of atoms by this value. If the simplest ratios calculated are not complete integers, multiply them by a common factor to get integer whole numbers of the simplest ratios. 4. Write symbols of all constituent atoms with their respective number of atoms as subscript to lower right-hand corner of the symbol. Thus, We get empirical formula of the compound. Determination of molecular formula : To determine the molecular formula, follow the steps used in finding empirical formula. Determine the empirical mass. If empirical and molecular masses of the compound are same, the empirical and molecular formulae will be same.
